evidence.claim: On Route 56, the Tye River Turnpike enters George Washington National Forest and winds up the Blue Ridge Mountains beside Little Marys Creek.
evidence.quote: SR 56 heads southeast into Rockbridge County as Tye River Turnpike, which enters George Washington National Forest and passes under Norfolk Southern Railway's Roanoke District at the village of Vesuvius.  The state highway follows Little Marys Creek along its winding ascent of the Blue Ridge Mountains.

evidence.claim: The climb reaches Tye River Gap, where Route 56 crosses into Nelson County and becomes Crabtree Falls Highway. Beyond the Parkway junction, the highway descends through Montebello toward the Tye River.
evidence.quote: SR 56 intersects the Blue Ridge Parkway at Tye River Gap, where the highway enters Nelson County and becomes Crabtree Falls Highway.  The state highway descends through Montebello and follows the South Fork of the Tye River

evidence.claim: Before the interstates, US 11 was the main long-distance road through western Virginia.
evidence.quote: Prior to the construction of the Interstate Highway System, it was the primary long-distance route for traversing the western part of the state.

evidence.claim: Its numbered identity came in 1926, after the corridor had entered the state highway system in 1918 under earlier route numbers.
evidence.quote: What is now US 11 was added to the state highway system in 1918 as portions of SR 10 (Bristol to Roanoke) and SR 3 (Roanoke to West Virginia). SR 3 became SR 33 in 1923, and US 11 was applied to its present alignment in 1926.

evidence.claim: Much of US 11 roughly follows the Great Wagon Road, the colonial route along the Appalachians from Georgia to Pennsylvania.
evidence.quote: Much of it roughly follows the Great Wagon Road, a colonial-era road that followed the Appalachian Mountains from Georgia to Pennsylvania.

evidence.claim: Most of US 11 now closely parallels I-81, following much the same alignment it received in 1926.
evidence.quote: Most of the route closely parallels I-81.

evidence.claim: following much the same alignment it received in 1926.
evidence.quote: it was first designated through Virginia in 1926 and has largely followed the same route since.

evidence.quote: Natural Bridge is located at the junction of U.S. Route 11 and State Route 130.

evidence.claim: That river forms Lexington’s northeastern boundary, while US 11 and US 60 meet in the city.
evidence.quote: The Maury River, a tributary of the James River, forms the city's northeastern boundary.

evidence.claim: US 11 and US 60 meet in the city.
evidence.quote: Lexington is located at the intersection of historic U.S. Route 11 and U.S. Route 60

evidence.claim: Lexington took its name in 1778 from Lexington, Massachusetts, the Revolutionary War namesake.
evidence.quote: Lexington was named in 1778. It was the second of what would be many American places named after Lexington, Massachusetts, known for being the place at which the first shot was fired in the American Revolution.

evidence.claim: It is home to Virginia Military Institute and Washington and Lee University.
evidence.quote: Lexington is best known as the home of the Virginia Military Institute and Washington and Lee University.

evidence.claim: On the Washington and Lee campus, a statue commemorates Cyrus McCormick, whose mechanical reaper was developed at his family’s Rockbridge County farm.
evidence.quote: Cyrus McCormick invented the horse-drawn mechanical reaper at his family's farm in Rockbridge County, and a statue of McCormick is located on the Washington and Lee University campus.

evidence.claim: The city’s downtown historic district and the George C. Marshall Library are among its historic destinations.
evidence.quote: Places of interest in Lexington include the Stonewall Jackson House, University Chapel, the George C. Marshall Library, Virginia Military Institute Museum, Museum of Military Memorabilia, and the downtown historic district.

evidence.claim: From US 11, fences obscure the limestone arch carrying the road.
evidence.quote: U.S. Route 11 (Lee Highway) runs on top of the bridge, but protective fences make it difficult to see anything besides the roadway.

evidence.claim: Below is a different scale: Natural Bridge rises 215 feet and spans 90 feet in the gorge carved by Cedar Creek.
evidence.quote: comprising a 215-foot-high (66 m) natural arch with a span of 90 feet (27 m). It is situated within a gorge carved from the surrounding mountainous limestone terrain by Cedar Creek

evidence.claim: Edgar W. Spencer interpreted the arch as the surviving roof of an underground river tunnel.
evidence.quote: According to Spencer, the Natural Bridge was the remnant of an underground river tunnel that diverted water to the south.

evidence.claim: The surrounding property became a state park in 2016.
evidence.quote: Natural Bridge State Park officially opened on September 24, 2016.

evidence.claim: Its Cedar Creek trail passes beneath the bridge and continues to the 30-foot Lace Falls.
evidence.quote: The state park includes several long-standing attractions, including the trail under the bridge along Cedar Creek and the 30-foot-tall (9.1 m) Lace Falls.

evidence.claim: Thomas Jefferson purchased the bridge and surrounding land in 1774, then built a two-room cabin with a room reserved for guests.
evidence.quote: Thomas Jefferson purchased 157 acres (64 ha) of land including the Natural Bridge from King George III of Great Britain for 20 shillings in 1774.

evidence.claim: then built a two-room cabin with a room reserved for guests.
evidence.quote: Jefferson built a two-room log cabin, with one room reserved for guests

evidence.claim: The blacksmith shop at Walnut Grove served two purposes: repairing the family’s farm implements and developing Cyrus McCormick’s reaper.
evidence.quote: The blacksmith shop was used to build and repair all the farm implements needed by the McCormick family and was where Cyrus McCormick engineered his reaper.

evidence.claim: McCormick improved and patented the machine, a predecessor of the combine harvester.
evidence.quote: Cyrus Hall McCormick improved and patented the mechanical reaper, which eventually led to the creation of the combine harvester.

evidence.claim: Eight original buildings survive, including the shop, grist mill and quarters for people enslaved by the McCormick family.
evidence.quote: The eight existing buildings include a grist mill, blacksmith shop, slave quarters, carriage house, manor house, smoke house, schoolroom, and housekeeper's quarters.

evidence.claim: The family enslaved forty-one people here.
evidence.quote: Slave quarters served as the homes for the forty-one slaves that the McCormick family owned.

evidence.claim: In 1847, Cyrus moved his operations to Chicago; the farm later became a museum run by Virginia Tech’s agricultural experimental station.
evidence.quote: Cyrus McCormick moved his base of operations from Rockbridge County, Virginia to Chicago, Illinois in 1847

evidence.claim: the farm later became a museum run by Virginia Tech’s agricultural experimental station.
evidence.quote: is currently a museum run by the Virginia Agricultural Experimental Station of Virginia Tech.

evidence.claim: The farm’s schoolroom holds textbooks, toys and other school supplies dating from the 1830s.
evidence.quote: The schoolroom is stocked with vintage textbooks, toys, and other school supplies dating from the 1830s.

flags: The cached List of Virginia Byways lacks its route table. Specific designation, date, boundaries and designating-body rationale cannot be verified; the catalog designation is not repeated as fact.
No turnpike construction history is cached. Overview history concerns US 11 only and does not equate it with the Great Wagon Road.

This record covers separate road sections. Moment sequence retains Lexington to Natural Bridge, followed by the farm near the start of Route 56; only Vesuvius has strip mileage. No connecting scenic segment is asserted.
Natural Bridge geology is an interpretation attributed to Spencer, not a settled formation account. No primary geological or Monacan community source is cached.
Farm donation dates conflict: the farm page says 1954, while Raphine says the 1960s. Donation date omitted.
Current story and moments have no motifs fields. Farm scene retains prairie as the closest available field category for agricultural land, not a claim of prairie ecology.
